questions.html:
Consider the $\textbf{Context-Free Grammar (CFG)}$ defined by the production rules:
$$
S \rightarrow S S+|S S *| a
$$
Which of the following statements regarding the properties of this grammar and its generated language are $\textbf{CORRECT}$?

options.html: The grammar is unambiguous because every string in the language possesses a unique leftmost derivation.
The language generated consists of all valid arithmetic expressions in prefix notation using the operand $a$.
The grammar is ambiguous as it allows for multiple parse trees for the string $a a+a *$.
The language generated is the set of all valid postfix expressions over the alphabet $\{a,+, *\}$.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

$\textbf{1. Analysis of the Language (Option B and D)}$

The production rules $S \rightarrow S S+$ and $S \rightarrow S S *$ indicate that an operator (+ or *) always follows two operands ( $S$ ). This structural pattern is the defining characteristic of $\textbf{Postfix Notation}$ (Reverse Polish Notation).

  • Example: The expression $(a+a) * a$ is represented in this grammar as $a a+a *$.
  • Since the operators are at the end of the sub-expressions, Option D is correct and Option B (Prefix) is incorrect.


$\textbf{2. Analysis of Ambiguity (Option A and C)}$

A grammar is ambiguous if there exists at least one string that has more than one distinct parse tree. For postfix expressions involving binary operators, the structure is strictly determined by the position of the operators.
To derive $a a+a *$ :

  • $\textbf{Leftmost Derivation}$: $S \Rightarrow S S * \Rightarrow S S+S * \Rightarrow a S+S * \Rightarrow a a+S * \Rightarrow a a+a *$


No other sequence of rule applications can produce this string. Because the grammar uniquely determines the grouping of operands with their respective operators, it is $\textbf{unambiguous}$.

$\textbf{Parse Tree Visualization}$:
 



Since the tree is unique, Option $\mathbf{A}$ is correct and Option $\mathbf{C}$ is incorrect.

Consider the following grammar for boolean expressions:

                                      $\,bexpr \to bexpr\ or\ bterm \mid bterm$

                                      $\,bterm \to bterm\ and\ bfactor \mid bfactor$

                                      $\,bfactor \to not\ bfactor \mid (bexpr) \mid true \mid false$

Which of the following statements regarding this grammar are $\textbf{CORRECT}$?

options.html: The operator and has higher precedence than or because it is defined further down the hierarchy of productions.
The expression true or false and false is ambiguous as it can result in two different truth values depending on the derivation.
The grammar is left-recursive, making the operators or and and left-associative.
The string not true and false is interpreted by the grammar as (not true) and false.

$\textbf{ Precedence (Option A \& D):}$

The grammar forces $not$ to be evaluated before $and$, and $and$ before $or$.

  • LMD for $not\ true\ and\ false:$

\[
bexpr \Rightarrow bterm \Rightarrow bterm\ and\ bfactor
\Rightarrow bfactor\ and\ bfactor
\Rightarrow not\ bfactor\ and\ bfactor
\Rightarrow not\ true\ and\ false
\]

  • This forces the $not$ to bind only to $true$, confirming Option D.

$\textbf{Associativity (Option C):}$

The rule $bexpr \to bexpr\ or\ bterm$ is left-recursive. This forces the parse tree to grow to the left.

Example for $true\ or\ true\ or\ false:$

\Rightarrow (bexpr\ or\ bterm)\ or\ bterm

questions.html:
Consider the Context-Free Grammar (CFG) $G$ defined by the following production rules:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \rightarrow 0 \mid A \\
& A \rightarrow A B \\
& B \rightarrow 1
\end{aligned}
$$
After applying the algorithm to eliminate all $\textbf{useless symbols}$ (symbols that are either nongenerating or unreachable), which of the following represents the resulting simplified grammar?

options.html: $S \rightarrow 0 \mid A, \quad A \rightarrow A B, \quad B \rightarrow 1$
$S \rightarrow 0, \quad B \rightarrow 1$
$S \rightarrow 0$
$S \rightarrow 0, \quad A \rightarrow A B$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

To eliminate useless symbols, we must perform two distinct phases in a specific order. A symbol is useful if and only if it is both $\textbf{Generating}$ and $\textbf{Reachable}$.

$\textbf{Phase\ 1:\ Elimination\ of\ Non\text{-}Generating\ Symbols}$

A symbol is generating if it can eventually derive a string of terminals.

$\textbf{Basis}$: Terminals $\{0,1\}$ are generating.
 

$\textbf{Iteration 1}$:

\[
S \to 0 \quad (0\ is\ generating)\ \Longrightarrow\ S\ is\ generating.
\]

\[
B \to 1 \quad (1\ is\ generating)\ \Longrightarrow\ B\ is\ generating.
\]

\[
A \to AB \quad (A\ is\ not\ yet\ known\ to\ be\ generating,\ so\ we\ cannot\ conclude\ A\ is\ generating).
\]

$\textbf{Iteration 2}$: No new symbols can be added because the only rule for $A$ is $A \to AB$, and since $A$ never reaches a terminal string, it is non-generating.

$\textbf{Generating\ Symbols:}\ \{S,B,0,1\}$

$\textbf{Remove $A$ and all productions containing $A$}$:

\[
S \to 0
\]

\[
B \to 1
\]

$\textbf{Phase\ 2:\ Elimination\ of\ Unreachable\ Symbols}$

A symbol is reachable if it can be reached from the start symbol $S$.

$\textbf{Basis$: $S$ is reachable.

$\textbf{Iteration 1}$: From $S \to 0$, the terminal $0$ is reachable.

$\textbf{Iteration 2}$: There are no other rules originating from $S$.

$\textbf{Result:}$ The symbol $B$ and the terminal $1$ are unreachable from the start symbol $S$.

$\textbf{Final\ Simplified\ Grammar:}$

After removing non-generating symbols first, and then unreachable symbols:

\[
S \to 0
\]

$\textbf{Note:}$ If you reversed the order (checking Reachability before Generating), you might incorrectly conclude that $B$ is useful. However, because $A$ is non-generating, any path from $S$ to $B$ via $A$ is “broken,” making the entire branch useless.

questions.html:
Consider the following Context-Free Grammar (CFG), which includes an $\epsilon$ (epsilon) production for the non-terminal $A$ :
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \rightarrow A B \$ \\
& A \rightarrow x A|B| \epsilon \\
& B \rightarrow y z B \mid z
\end{aligned}
$$
With the addition of the rule $A \rightarrow \epsilon$, is the grammar still an LL(1) grammar? Choose the correct classification and justification.

options.html: Yes, the grammar remains $\operatorname{LL}(1)$ because $\operatorname{FIRST}(\epsilon)=\{\epsilon\}$, which is disjoint from $\operatorname{First}(x A)$ and $\operatorname{FiRST}(B)$.
No, the grammar is no longer $\mathrm{LL}(1)$ because adding $A \rightarrow \epsilon$ creates a FIRST-FIRST conflict between $A \rightarrow x A$ and $A \rightarrow B$.
No, the grammar is no longer $\mathrm{LL}(1)$ because the addition of $A \rightarrow \epsilon$ introduces a FIRST-FOLLOW conflict for non-terminal $A$ on lookaheads $y$ and $z$.
Yes, the grammar remains $\mathrm{LL}(1)$ because $\operatorname{FOLLOW}(A)=\{\$\}$, which does not intersect with the FIRST sets of $A$ 's other productions.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

To determine if the grammar is LL$(1)$, we must calculate the FIRST and FOLLOW sets to check for conflicts.

$\textbf{Step\ 1:\ Calculate\ FIRST\ sets}$

\[
First(B)=\{y,z\}
\]

\[
First(A)=\{x\}\cup First(B)\cup \{\epsilon\}=\{x,y,z,\epsilon\}
\]

\[
First(S)=First(A)\setminus\{\epsilon\}\cup First(B)=\{x,y,z\}
\]

$\textbf{Step\ 2:\ Calculate\ FOLLOW\ sets}$

\[
Follow(S)=\{\$\}
\]

\[
Follow(A)=First(B)=\{y,z\}
\qquad
(\text{from the production } S\to AB\$)
\]

\[
Follow(B)=\{\$\}\cup Follow(A)=\{y,z,\$\}
\qquad
(\text{from } S\to AB\$ \text{ and } A\to B)
\]

Let us number the productions to populate the table:

$1)\ S\to AB$

$2)\ A\to xA$

$3)\ A\to B$

$4)\ B\to yzB$

$5)\ B\to z$

$6)\ A\to \epsilon$

We place the productions into the table $M[N,T]$ based on the FIRST sets. If a non-terminal has an $\epsilon$-production, we place that $\epsilon$-production in the columns corresponding to its FOLLOW set.

\[
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & x & y & z & \$ \\
\hline
S & 1 & 1 & 1 & \\
\hline
A & 2 & 3,6 & 3,6 & \\
\hline
B & & 4 & 5 & \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

$\textbf{Conclusion:}$

As seen in the parsing table, there are multiple entries for $M[A,y]$ and $M[A,z]$.

$\bullet$ The production $A\to B$ (Rule $3$) is placed under $y$ and $z$ because they are in $FIRST(B)$.

$\bullet$ The production $A\to \epsilon$ (Rule $6$) is also placed under $y$ and $z$ because they are in $FOLLOW(A)$.

If the parser is expanding $A$ and sees a $y$ or $z$, it does not know whether to substitute $B$ or to remove $A$. This is a classic FIRST-FOLLOW conflict, meaning the grammar is not LL$(1)$.

questions.html:
Consider the standard algorithm for eliminating left recursion from a contextfree grammar $G$ (given that $G$ initially has no cycles or $\epsilon$-productions), as detailed below:

$\textbf{Algorithm}$: Eliminating left recursion

  1. arrange the nonterminals in some order $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$.
  2.  for (each $i$ from 1 to $n$ ) {
  3.  for (each $j$ from 1 to $i-1$ ) {
  4. replace each production of the form $A_{i} \rightarrow A_{j} \gamma$ by the productions $A_{i} \rightarrow \delta_{1} \gamma\left|\delta_{2} \gamma\right| \cdots \mid \delta_{k} \gamma$, where $A_{j} \rightarrow \delta_{1}\left|\delta_{2}\right| \cdots \mid \delta_{k}$ are all current $A_{j}$-productions
  5.  }
  6.  eliminate the immediate left recursion among the $A_{i}$-productions
  7. }

In the context of this algorithm, what is the fundamental computational purpose of the core inner logic executed inside the $j$ 's for loop (specifically, the substitution happening in Step $4$)?

options.html: It eliminates immediate left recursion for the nonterminal $A_{i}$ directly by introducing new primed nonterminals.
It removes $\epsilon$-productions from the grammar to ensure the resulting grammar adheres to the strict constraints of top-down parsing.
It converts indirect left recursion into immediate left recursion by substituting the expanded bodies of previously processed $A_{j}$-productions into the current $A_{i}$-productions.
It reorders the grammar's nonterminals dynamically during runtime to guarantee that $A_{i}$ always derives strings that strictly begin with a terminal symbol.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

The overall goal of the algorithm is to eliminate all left recursion, both immediate and indirect.

  • Step $6$ handles the immediate left recursion (where a production looks like $A_{i} \rightarrow A_{i} \alpha$ ).
     
  • However, if there is indirect left recursion (for example, $A_{1} \rightarrow A_{2} \alpha$ and $A_{2} \rightarrow A_{1} \beta$ ), Step 6 alone cannot detect it.
     

The inner $j$'s loop (Steps $3$ through $5$) solves this by enforcing a strict ordering. Because $j<i$, the algorithm guarantees that by the time it evaluates $A_i$, all nonterminals before it ($A_1$ through $A_{i-1}$) have already been fully processed and freed of left recursion. By substituting the right-hand side of $A_j$ into $A_i$ (Step $4$), any hidden indirect left-recursive chains are forced to the surface, transforming them into immediate left recursion on $A_i$. Once exposed, Step $6$ can successfully eliminate it.

questions.html:
Consider the following Context-Free Grammar (CFG) representing the "dangling-else" problem for conditional statements:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& S \rightarrow i E t S|i E t S e S| a \\
& E \rightarrow b
\end{aligned}
$$
(where $i, t, e$ stand for $\textbf{if, then, else}$, and $a, b$ are other terminals).

To make this grammar suitable for top-down predictive parsing, we must eliminate non-determinism by applying $\textbf{left-factoring}$. Which of the following represents the correct grammar after applying the left-factoring algorithm?

options.html:
$S \rightarrow i E t S^{\prime} \mid a$
$S^{\prime} \rightarrow S \mid S e S$
$E \rightarrow b$

$S \rightarrow i E t S S^{\prime} \mid a$
$S^{\prime} \rightarrow e S \mid \epsilon$
$E \rightarrow b$

$S \rightarrow i E t S S^{\prime} e S \mid a$
$S^{\prime} \rightarrow \epsilon$
$E \rightarrow b$

$S \rightarrow i E S^{\prime} \mid a$
$S^{\prime} \rightarrow t S \mid t S e S$
$E \rightarrow b$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

$\textbf{Concept\ of\ Left\text{-}Factoring:}$

Left-factoring is a grammar transformation used to resolve situations where two or more productions for the same non-terminal share a common prefix. This shared prefix makes it impossible for a predictive parser (like an LL($1$) parser) to know which production to choose by looking only at the next input token.

The general rule for left-factoring is: If we have productions

\[
A \to \alpha\beta_1 \mid \alpha\beta_2 \mid \cdots \mid \alpha\beta_n \mid \gamma,
\]

where $\alpha$ is the longest common prefix (and $\alpha \neq \epsilon$), we replace them with:

\[
A \to \alpha A' \mid \gamma
\]

\[
A' \to \beta_1 \mid \beta_2 \mid \cdots \mid \beta_n
\]

$\textbf{Application\ to\ the\ Given\ Grammar:}$

Look at the productions for $S$:

\[
S \to iEtS \mid iEtSeS \mid a
\]

$1.$ $\textbf{Identify\ the\ longest\ common\ prefix\ }(\alpha):$

Both $iEtS$ and $iEtSeS$ start with the sequence $iEtS$.

Therefore,

\[
\alpha = iEtS
\]

$2.$ $\textbf{Identify\ the\ remainders\ }(\beta):$

For the first production $(iEtS)$, the remainder after the prefix is empty. So,

\[
\beta_1 = \epsilon
\]

For the second production $(iEtSeS)$, the remainder after the prefix is $eS$. So,

\[
\beta_2 = eS
\]

$3.$ $\textbf{Identify\ the\ alternatives\ }(\gamma):$

The production $S \to a$ does not share the prefix. So,

\[
\gamma = a
\]

Applying the transformation: Replace the $S$ productions with:

\[
S \to (iEtS)S' \mid a
\]

\[
S' \to \epsilon \mid eS
\]

$\textbf{Analysis\ of\ Incorrect\ Options:}$

$\textbf{Option\ A:}$ This factors out $iEt$, not the longest common prefix. While technically it factors the grammar, standard left-factoring requires pulling out the maximum common prefix to fully resolve the parsing decision for that sequence.

$\textbf{Option\ C:}$ This fundamentally changes the language generated by the grammar.

$\textbf{Option\ D:}$ Similar to A, it only factors out $iE$, which leaves common prefixes $(tS)$ in the resulting $S'$ productions, failing to solve the problem completely.

Consider the following context-free grammar:

$$
S \rightarrow S+S|S S|(S)|S *| a
$$
Left factoring is a grammar transformation technique used to resolve FIRSTset conflicts when multiple productions for the same non-terminal share a common prefix. If you apply the standard left factoring algorithm to this grammar, which of the following represents the correct transformed grammar?

options.html:
$S\to(S)S'\mid aS'$
$S'\to+SS'\mid SS'\mid *S\mid\epsilon$

$S\to SS'\mid(S)\mid a$
 $S'\to+S\mid S\mid *\mid\epsilon$

$S\to SS'\mid(S)\mid a$
 $S'\to+S\mid S\mid *$

$S\to S+S'\mid SS'\mid(S)\mid a$
 $S'\to S\mid *$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

To left factor a grammar, we look for productions of a non-terminal that share a common prefix. The standard form to look for is

\[
A \to \alpha\beta_1 \mid \alpha\beta_2 \mid \cdots \mid \alpha\beta_n \mid \gamma,
\]

where $\alpha$ is the common prefix (and $\alpha \neq \epsilon$). We transform this into:

\[
A \to \alpha A' \mid \gamma
\]

\[
A' \to \beta_1 \mid \beta_2 \mid \cdots \mid \beta_n
\]

$\textbf{Analyzing\ the\ given\ grammar's\ alternatives\ for\ } S:$

$1.$ $S+S$ (starts with $S$)

$2.$ $SS$ (starts with $S$)

$3.$ $(S)$ (does not start with $S$)

$4.$ $S*$ (starts with $S$)

$5.$ $a$ (does not start with $S$)

The common prefix $\alpha$ among the first, second, and fourth alternatives is clearly $S$.

Let’s factor out this common prefix $S$:

$\bullet$ From $S+S$, if we extract prefix $S$, the remainder $(\beta_1)$ is $+S$

$\bullet$ From $SS$, if we extract prefix $S$, the remainder $(\beta_2)$ is $S$

$\bullet$ From $S*$, if we extract prefix $S$, the remainder $(\beta_3)$ is $*$

The alternatives that do not share the prefix $(\gamma)$ are $(S)$ and $a$.

Applying the transformation rule, we introduce a new non-terminal $S'$ to derive the remainders:

\[
S \to SS' \mid (S) \mid a
\]

\[
S' \to +S \mid S \mid *
\]

$\textit{Note\ on\ Distractors:}$

$\bullet$ Option A represents the grammar after $\textit{Immediate\ Left\ Recursion\ Elimination}$, not left factoring.

$\bullet$ Option B incorrectly includes an $\epsilon$-production in $S'$. An $\epsilon$ is only added if one of the original alternatives is exactly the prefix itself (e.g., if we had $S \to S+S \mid S$, then factoring $S$ leaves $\epsilon$). Here, the alternative is $SS$, so factoring out $S$ leaves $S$, not $\epsilon$.

Consider the grammar:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text { rexp } & \rightarrow \text { rexp }+ \text { rterm } \mid \text { rterm } \\
\text { rterm } & \rightarrow \text { rterm } r \text { factor } \mid \text { rfactor } \\
\text { rfactor } & \rightarrow \text { rfactor } * \mid \text { rprimary } \\
\text { rprimary } & \rightarrow a \mid b
\end{aligned}
$$
Which of the following grammars is obtained after removing left recursion?

options.html:
$rexp\to rterm\ rexp'$
$rexp'\to +\ rterm\ rexp'\mid \epsilon$
$rterm\to rfactor\ rterm'$
$rterm'\to rfactor\ rterm'\mid \epsilon$
$rfactor\to rprimary\ rfactor'$
$rfactor'\to *\ rfactor'\mid \epsilon$
$rprimary\to a\mid b$

$rexp\to rexp+rterm\mid rterm$
$rterm\to rfactor\ rterm$
$rterm'\to rfactor\mid \epsilon$
$rfactor\to rprimary*\mid rprimary$
$rprimary\to a\mid b$

$rexp\to +\ rterm\ rexp'\mid rterm$
$rexp'\to rexp\mid \epsilon$
$rterm\to rfactor$
$rfactor\to rprimary\mid rprimary$
$rprimary\to a\mid b$

$rexp\to rterm+rexp\mid rterm$
$rterm\to rfactor\ rterm\mid *rfactor$
$rfactor\to rprimary*\mid rprimary$
$rprimary\to a\mid b$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

For a production of the form
$$
A \rightarrow \Lambda \alpha \mid \beta
$$
the left recursion is removed using:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& A \rightarrow \beta A^{\prime} \\
& A^{\prime} \rightarrow \alpha A^{\prime} \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying this transformation:
$$
\text { rexp  rexp + rterm } \mid \text { rterm }
$$
becomes
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { rexp } \rightarrow \text { rterm rexp } \\
& \text { rexp } \rightarrow+\text { rterm rexp }{ }^{\prime} \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { rterm } \rightarrow r \text { factor rterm }{ }^{\prime} \\
& \text { rterm }^{\prime} \rightarrow r \text { factor } \text { rterm }^{\prime} \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$
and
$$
\begin{aligned}
& r \text { factor } \rightarrow \text { rprimary } r \text { factor }^{\prime} \\
& \text { rfactor }^{\prime} \rightarrow * \text { factor }^{\prime} \mid \epsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, Option A is correct.

& \operatorname{Follow}(S)=\{ \} \\
& \operatorname{Follow}(A)=\{\$, x, w\} \\
& \operatorname{Follow}(B)=\{y, z\} \\
& \operatorname{Follow}(C)=\{\$, x, y, z, w\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let us number the productions for the parsing table: 1) $S \rightarrow A \$  2) A \rightarrow x A x$ 3) $A \rightarrow C$ 4) $B \rightarrow y B y$ 5) $B \rightarrow C$ 6) $C \rightarrow z B z$ 7) $C \rightarrow w A w$ 8) $C \rightarrow \epsilon$

$\textbf{LL(1) Parsing Table:}$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
 & x & y & z & w & \$ \\
\hline
S & \begin{array}{c}1\end{array} &  & \begin{array}{c}1\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}1\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}1\end{array} \\
\hline
A & \begin{array}{c}2,3\end{array} &  & \begin{array}{c}3\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}3\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}3\end{array} \\
\hline
B &  & \begin{array}{c}4,5\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}5\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}5\end{array} &  \\
\hline
C & \begin{array}{c}8\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}8\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}6,8\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}7,8\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}8\end{array} \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$

This is not an $\mathrm{LL}(1)$ grammar, because there are conflicts in the parse table (e.g., multiple entries in $M[A, x], M[B, y], M[C, z]$, and $M[C, w]$ ). These are FIRST-FOLLOW conflicts arising because non-terminals like $A, B$, and $C$ are nullable (they can derive $\epsilon$ ), and their FIRST sets intersect with their FOLLOW sets.
